sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Event-driven architecture is central to modern microservices, and Kafka is the dominant durable message broker while NATS is the dominant lightweight pub/sub and queue solution in Go-heavy cloud-native stacks. Interviewers probe this module to verify you understand the Kafka consumer group model (partition assignment, rebalancing, offset management), the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, and why NATS JetStream was introduced to give NATS durability. Showing you know the tradeoffs between confluent-kafka-go and sarama — and when to pick each — demonstrates real production experience with messaging systems.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Kafka partitions a topic across brokers; each partition is an ordered, append-only log. A consumer group is a set of Go processes that collectively consume all partitions of a topic — each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group at a time. When a consumer joins or leaves, Kafka triggers a rebalance, reassigning partitions. Offsets track how far each consumer group has read; committing an offset is how you record progress. confluent-kafka-go is a CGO wrapper around librdkafka — high performance, lower-level. sarama is a pure Go implementation — easier to cross-compile, more idiomatic, slightly lower throughput. NATS core is a fire-and-forget pub/sub — no persistence. JetStream adds subjects with persistence, replay, and consumer acknowledgement, making NATS suitable for exactly-once-style workloads.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. confluent-kafka-go producer — kafka.NewProducer, p.Produce(msg, deliveryChan), poll the deliveryChan for acks; set acks=all for durability. 2. sarama consumer group — implement ConsumerGroupHandler (Setup, Cleanup, ConsumeClaim); the Consume loop re-calls Setup/Cleanup on every rebalance. 3. Consumer group rebalance triggers — consumer joins, consumer crashes, topic partition count changes; RangeAssignor vs RoundRobinAssignor strategies. 4. Offset management — auto-commit is convenient but risks re-processing or data loss; manual commit after processing guarantees at-least-once. 5. Kafka error handling — partition-level errors, broker disconnects; dead-letter topic pattern for poison messages. 6. NATS pub/sub — nc.Publish / nc.Subscribe; QueueSubscribe for load-balanced delivery across a group. 7. NATS JetStream — js.AddStream(cfg), js.Publish, js.Subscribe with durable consumer name; ack modes (AckExplicit, AckAll). 8. NATS vs Kafka tradeoffs — NATS: low latency, simple operations, no ZooKeeper; Kafka: high throughput, long retention, replay semantics.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: What triggers a Kafka consumer group rebalance and how does it affect your application? — Rebalances are triggered by consumer join/leave or partition count changes; during rebalance all consumption pauses; long processing loops must commit offsets before the rebalance deadline or the partition is revoked mid-processing. Q: What is the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once delivery in Kafka? — At-least-once: commit after processing; a crash before commit causes re-delivery. Exactly-once requires idempotent producers + transactional producers + read-committed consumers. Q: Why would you choose sarama over confluent-kafka-go? — Pure Go means easy cross-compilation (no CGO) and simpler Docker images; confluent-kafka-go offers higher throughput via librdkafka but requires C build tooling. Q: How does NATS JetStream differ from core NATS? — Core NATS is fire-and-forget with no persistence; JetStream adds stream storage, message replay, consumer groups, and acknowledgement-based delivery. Q: How do you handle a poison message in Kafka? — Catch the processing error, publish the raw message to a dead-letter topic with error metadata, commit the original offset to unblock the consumer.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "For high-throughput event pipelines where we need long retention and replay — like audit logs or event sourcing — I use Kafka with sarama's consumer group interface. I always manage offsets manually: process the message, persist the result, then commit the offset; auto-commit can lose messages if the process crashes between receiving and committing. I implement ConsumeClaim in a way that respects the rebalance deadline — if processing takes more than the session timeout, Kafka will revoke the partition and double-process. For lighter-weight internal messaging where I just need fan-out or work queue semantics without the operational overhead of a Kafka cluster, I use NATS JetStream — it gives me durable, acknowledged delivery with a much simpler deployment. In both cases I have a dead-letter topic or stream for poison messages so a single bad payload doesn't block the entire consumer."
